messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Rabbi
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid Sex: Sex, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina, a 48-year-old African American woman who served as a rabbi in her community, had built a life that was outwardly steady and deeply structured around caring for others. That steadiness was interrupted when a man-made disaster struck in a public place she knew well, turning an ordinary day into one marked by the force of a sudden explosion and the confusion that followed. In her account, the blast came without warning, a sharp bang that seemed to split the air and freeze everyone in place. What stayed with her most was not only the sound itself but the immediate sense that the world had become unsafe in an instant, that something human-made had erupted into the middle of life and could do so again at any time. From that day on, the memory of the event remained vivid enough that even hearing a loud bang in another context could pull her back into the same startled dread.

In the weeks and months afterward, Amina found herself responding to the world as though danger might be hidden in ordinary moments. She became acutely unsettled by explosion or bang sounds, whether they came from construction outside her synagogue, a dropped object in a kitchen, or something sudden on television. She also noticed a disturbing sense of being watched, as if eyes were on her even in familiar places. That feeling could arise while she was walking through her neighborhood or sitting in her office, and she would have to work to keep her composure while continuing with her responsibilities. News about violence or disasters was especially hard to take in. When a related story came on the radio or appeared on her phone, she would often put it aside quickly, not wanting the images or headlines to settle into her mind. She had come to expect that hearing about similar events could leave her tense for the rest of the day.

Amina’s day-to-day life gradually narrowed around efforts to keep herself from being reminded of what had happened. When friends, congregants, or colleagues mentioned the event or something similar, she would try to change the subject or leave the room, and afterward she often felt drained and irritated with herself for being unable to sit through the conversation. At home, she avoided sex with her husband, not because she no longer cared for him, but because intimacy left her feeling exposed in a way she could not tolerate. She described a need to stay in control of her body and surroundings, and sexual closeness felt too vulnerable, too likely to let in feelings she was trying to keep contained. Over time, this created distance in the marriage that she found painful to acknowledge, though she did not know how to explain that the problem was not her husband but the sense of danger that followed her into private moments.

Her sense of safety also changed in quieter, more persistent ways. Amina reported that even when others told her she was safe, she found it impossible to believe them. She could hear the reassurance and understand it intellectually, but it did not reach the part of her that remained on alert. Nighttime was especially difficult. During the day she could sometimes keep herself occupied, but after dark she became more watchful and found it harder to settle. She checked doors, listened for unusual sounds, and remained sensitive to the possibility that something could happen again when the house was quiet. She constantly scanned her surroundings for signs of danger, a habit that became part of how she moved through the world and through her work. As a rabbi, she was often in shared spaces—meeting with congregants, attending services, moving through hallways and parking lots—and she found herself automatically looking for exits, noting who was near her, and noticing abrupt noises before anyone else seemed to react. She could not stop mentally assessing whether something looked off.

Alongside this vigilance came a harsh way of thinking about herself and the event. Amina repeatedly told herself that she would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. She returned again and again to what she had done and what she had failed to do in those moments, measuring herself against what she believed she should have been able to change. At the same time, she had come to believe that she had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. That belief was not abstract; it shaped how she walked into buildings, how she sat in meetings, and how she moved through evenings at home. She also found herself thinking that nothing good could happen to her anymore, as if the disaster had marked a line beyond which ordinary hope no longer applied to her life. These thoughts sat alongside a persistent sense of apprehension that she described as exhausting but inescapable.

By the time she sought help, Amina was still functioning in many of her roles, but she was doing so in a narrowed, effortful way that left her feeling increasingly worn down. The final push came when the combination of news reports, sudden loud noises, and the strain of staying constantly on guard began to feel unmanageable, and when the distance in her marriage became harder for her to ignore. She came to treatment wanting relief from the sense that danger was always near and from the belief that the future held nothing good for her. What she feared most was being unable to trust safety even when it was offered, and what she hoped for, cautiously, was the chance to live and work without feeling as though she had to watch for the next disaster at every turn.
